blocks.title: The structure matters more than the drawing
paragraphs: A tree records parent/child structure, while a directed graph records ordered edges. Drawings help you see these relationships; the adjacency and child order determine the mathematics. State conventions before calculating or constructing.

These new examples use current normalized tree/graph scope and the current Lecture 11/14 associations. Historical Lecture 8 supplies no additional convention. For the binary trees here, left/right order is explicit and height counts edges: a leaf has height 0 and the empty tree height −1.

blocks.title: Read a labelled ordered binary tree
paragraphs: Use this tree: root M; M has left child G and right child T; G has no left child and has right child J; T has left child P and right child W; J, P and W have no children.

There are six nodes, three leaves (J,P,W), and height two edges. The proper descendants of G are just J. A construction must meet all requested conditions together: labels, node count, leaf count, height and any traversal constraints.

A child may have at most one parent in a tree, and all nodes must be reachable from the root without a cycle. Repositioning nodes on the page does not change the tree if these relationships remain fixed.

blocks.title: Track when the root is visited
paragraphs: Preorder visits root, left subtree, right subtree; inorder visits left subtree, root, right subtree; postorder visits left subtree, right subtree, root. These inorder instructions are for ordered binary trees. Empty child positions contribute no labels.
For the stated tree, preorder is M,G,J,T,P,W; inorder is G,J,M,P,T,W; postorder is J,G,P,W,T,M. At every recursive call use the same visiting rule, including a node with only a right child.

blocks.title: Define every tree-function case
paragraphs: Define node count by N(empty)=0 and N(node(value,left,right))=1+N(left)+N(right). The case split covers the empty tree and every nonempty ordered binary tree. It does not require both children to exist.

In the example, N(G)=1+0+1=2 and N(T)=1+1+1=3, so N(M)=1+2+3=6. A recursive transformation similarly needs an empty case and a node case; to mirror a binary tree, recursively mirror both subtrees and swap their left/right positions.

For height under our edge convention, H(empty)=−1 and H(node)=1+max(H(left),H(right)). Leaves therefore have height 0. Different height conventions need different bases; never silently transfer a result between them.

blocks.title: Construct against an explicit constraint list
paragraphs: Declare a finite vertex set and the permitted directed edges. Check node and edge counts, whether loops or duplicate edges are allowed, reachability if required, and all cycle/order requirements. In these examples graphs are simple and directed: no loops and no repeated edges.

To construct a DAG with a chosen topological order, add only edges pointing forward in that order. That ensures acyclicity, but other constraints still need separate checks. Multiple graphs may satisfy the same requirements; one reference drawing is not a unique answer.

blocks.title: An order respects every directed edge
paragraphs: For vertices {A,B,C,D} and edges A→C, B→C, C→D, a topological order must put A and B before C, and C before D. There are exactly two: A,B,C,D and B,A,C,D. A and B are unconstrained relative to each other.
A directed cycle makes topological ordering impossible: following each cycle edge would require a vertex to come before itself. Adding D→A to this example creates the cycle A→C→D→A.

A finite DAG admits an order by repeatedly removing a vertex with no incoming edge from the remaining vertices. If several choices exist, explore their different orderings rather than asserting uniqueness. Validate a proposed order by checking each vertex occurs once and every edge points from an earlier to a later position.

blocks.title: Counts alone do not establish structure
paragraphs: A node list and an edge count do not guarantee a tree; a cycle or a disconnected part can remain. A topological order need not be unique. Traversal answers depend on child order, while drawing angles and distances have no role in these definitions.

A finite tool checks the declared representation and constraints. Open tree, graph and recursive-function constructions still need a reasoned requirements check; matching one example is not proof of correctness.

blocks.title: Declare the structure, then apply one rule consistently
paragraphs: For trees, fix child order and the height convention, handle empty cases, and recurse consistently. For graphs, use explicit edges to establish acyclicity and check topological constraints. Verify a construction against every stated requirement.

cards.prompt: How do you check a tree construction beyond its picture?
cards.answer: Check one root, unique parents, reachability, no cycles, and every requested count, height, child-order and value constraint. Many different valid trees may satisfy the same task.

cards.prompt: When is a node visited in preorder, inorder and postorder?
cards.answer: Preorder: before its left and right subtrees. Inorder for a binary tree: between left and right. Postorder: after both. Empty children contribute nothing.

cards.prompt: What must be stated before giving the height of a tree?
cards.answer: Whether height counts edges or nodes, and how the empty tree is handled. In these examples a leaf has edge height 0 and the empty tree height −1.

cards.prompt: What makes a recursive tree-function definition complete?
cards.answer: It covers the empty structure and every constructor, specifies recursive calls on the required subtrees, and gives a result of the declared kind in each case.

cards.prompt: How can a chosen vertex order help construct a DAG?
cards.answer: Use only edges pointing forward in that order. A directed cycle would require an edge path to return to an earlier vertex. Still check every other construction requirement.

cards.prompt: What must a proposed topological order satisfy?
cards.answer: It lists every vertex exactly once and places the source of every directed edge before its target. This checks the actual edges, not geometric position.

cards.prompt: What do a directed cycle and multiple available source vertices imply?
cards.answer: A directed cycle prevents topological ordering. In a finite DAG, a choice between distinct currently available vertices allows different topological orders.

guided.title: Construct and justify a constrained tree
guided.prompt: Construct an ordered binary tree with six distinct labels, exactly three leaves and edge height two. State its child relationships and preorder. Any satisfying tree is allowed.
rubric: Every nonroot node has exactly one parent and the whole structure is connected and acyclic.
There are six nodes, three leaves and a longest root-to-leaf path of two edges.
Preorder consistently visits node, left, right.
reference: One reference is root M; left G with right child J; right T with children P and W. J,P,W are leaves.
This has six nodes, three leaves, height two and preorder M,G,J,T,P,W. Labels and shape may differ if every stated constraint holds.

guided.title: Define a mirror transformation
guided.prompt: Define a recursive transformation that mirrors an ordered binary tree. Explain the empty case and what happens at each nonempty node.
rubric: The empty tree maps to the empty tree.
At each node the transformed right subtree becomes the left subtree and vice versa.
Every original label occurs once in the result, and recursive calls handle descendants as well as the root.
reference: Swapping only the root children without recursively mirroring their interiors is incomplete. The result keeps labels and node count while reversing left/right structure at every node.

guided.title: Construct a DAG with two valid orders
guided.prompt: Construct a simple directed graph on {A,B,C,D} with exactly three edges and exactly two topological orders. Show both orders and justify that there are no others.
rubric: There are four vertices, three distinct directed edges, no loops, and no cycle.
Each stated ordering respects every edge.
The justification excludes all remaining permutations; producing two orders alone does not establish exactly two.
reference: A reference uses A→C, B→C, C→D. Both A and B must precede C, and C must precede D.
Only the relative order of A and B is free. Thus A,B,C,D and B,A,C,D are the only orders. Other graphs satisfying the full requirements are allowed.
